name: PT FKS Food Sejahtera Tbk

frontmatter.title: FKS Food Sejahtera: a cost-cycle trough and a governance discount priced as permanent
frontmatter.summary: AISA sells Taro snacks and Ayam Dua Telor noodles through a distributor under common control and trades below restated book after a year of flour-driven margin squeeze. We think the squeeze is a cost event, not a demand collapse; the counterweight is that the largest customer sets the margin. Base value is well above the quote and the bear case is about half of it.
thesis: The FY2026 profit decline is a wheat-cost event: revenue grew in both segments while cost of goods sold outran it, and the agri deck has the input easing from FY2028. The revenue itself is largely billed to an affiliate, so we lean on the cost side of that sentence and say so.

The equity trades below restated book value because the market discounts a legacy fraud, a related-party customer and a frozen anti-corruption escrow - but the bear case is worth Rp47 against a price of Rp97, so we hold the spread between Rp47 and Rp148, not a claim that downside has gone away.
The quasi-reorganisation that took effect in July 2026 removed the deficit that blocked distributions; a first dividend is the most likely next corporate action.
Earnings recover to about the operating margin the company earned in 2023-24, peak a fraction above it and then fade; the net gross margin the model prints never exceeds the FY2025 actual.

What kills it: a second year of high wheat with no shelf-price room, or a transfer-pricing decision at the affiliated distributor that moves profit away from the listed entity. Both are in the bear case rather than in a footnote.

blocks.text: **BUY**, target Rp172 against a last price of Rp97, a return of 77.2%. The target is the probability-weighted twelve-month value of the three scenarios, Rp191, less the liquidity discount of 10.0%; our base value per share before the roll is Rp148. The market is not disputing the quality of the Taro and Ayam Dua Telor franchises; it is pricing a company whose profit fell in 2026 while revenue rose, whose largest customer is an affiliated company, and whose balance sheet carries a frozen escrow from a corruption case about a legacy sukuk [S3].

The variant view is narrower than it looks. At Rp97 the shares change hands at 0.7x our FY2026E restated book value of 131.4 per share and at 11.6x FY2026E earnings that are themselves at a cost-cycle trough: cost of goods sold rose far faster than sales over the first nine months of 2026, cutting attributable profit even as revenue grew by double digits [S2][S3]. Our base case has the margin recovering to the level the company actually earned in FY2024, and nothing better.

Three things move the value. First, the wheat path: the agri deck carries FY2026E and FY2027E wheat at US$294/t against the latest World Bank Pink Sheet print of US$347/t for September, so the deck's forecast sits below the most recent tape rather than above it - the house view is that the September print is a weather and competing-oil premium that fades, not a level that persists [S0][S8]. Second, the pass-through lag: we calibrate it so the model reproduces the margin the company has actually reported for the first nine months of 2026 [S2][S3]. Third, the escrow: IDR150.0bn is frozen pending the criminal rulings, a large share of equity, and we carry half of it in the bridge as the probability-weighted value of the return, because it sits outside cash and outside the operating enterprise the DCF discounts [S3].

The honest counterweight is in the governance section, and it is why the target is not higher. Most of net sales go to a company under common control, so the listed entity's margin is partly a transfer-pricing outcome rather than a market outcome, and a minority holder is a price-taker on that decision [S3]. We do not claim the downside is absent: the bear case is worth Rp47, roughly half the quote, and it now carries the two risks this report names as dominant - a distributor margin reset and a wheat market that holds the September print - rather than only a slower recovery. The position is the spread: Rp47 against a base of Rp148 and a bull of Rp332 on a price of Rp97. The distribution is wide because the earnings base is thin: at a trough operating margin, a swing of a few points of gross margin doubles or halves operating profit, and no amount of target-setting changes that arithmetic.

PT FKS Food Sejahtera is an Indonesian packaged-food manufacturer listed on the exchange since the late nineties under the code AISA, formerly Tiga Pilar Sejahtera Food [S4]. It makes two things: extruded and wafer snacks under Taro and related brands, and staple foods - dry noodles under Ayam Dua Telor and Mie Kremezz, and rice vermicelli - sold into the mass market [S4][S5]. The split matters for the model: snacks were IDR1,252.7bn of gross sales in FY2025 and staple foods IDR811.9bn, before discounts and rebates of the order of a twentieth of gross sales [S3].

The company reports as a single food-industry segment but discloses the product split in the revenue note [S3]. Manufacturing is split across plants in Central Java, West Java and North Sumatra, with the noodle and snack lines concentrated at Sragen, the snack and wafer lines at Gunung Putri, and vermicelli and distribution at Tangerang [S4][S5]. The subsidiaries are almost wholly owned and include the operating companies behind each brand family plus a small captive power unit [S4].

The commercial model runs through third-party distributors rather than direct-to-retail: about 193,568 outlets reached by the distributor groups the company appoints across the main islands [S5]. That reach is the asset that produced the growth of 2026, and management now describes the strategic shift from expanding availability to optimising share within the outlets already covered [S4]. The annual report's marketing pillars are distribution precision, brand rejuvenation, affordable pack sizes for weaker purchasing power, and cross-brand promotion aimed at younger consumers [S4].

Ownership is concentrated. PT Pangan Sejahtera Investama holds 58.4% of the shares with voting rights and is disclosed as the controlling owner, directly and indirectly; the public holds 26.1% and a second family vehicle holds the balance [S4]. The group behind it is the FKS food and agri complex, which also owns the flour mill and the sugar refiner that supply this company - a fact that shapes both the cost base and the governance discussion in the governance section [S3].

The Indonesian packaged-snack aisle is a scale business: shelf space in general trade is won by distributor density and by price points that survive a weak rupiah, and the categories AISA competes in - extruded snacks, wafers, dry noodles, vermicelli - are contested by the large diversified food groups and by regional and private-label producers. Brand recall in these categories is durable but not exclusive, and the buyer is highly price-elastic at the bottom of the market, which is why pack-size engineering rather than headline price is the usual response to input inflation.

The company's own annual report cites an Indonesian food and beverage industry CAGR of 12.8% to 2031, driven by a young urban population, modern retail and convenience food [S4]. We treat that as a description of direction rather than a forecast: it is a third-party projection repeated in the annual report, and no listed food company in this market grows at that rate indefinitely. What we can verify is that this company's revenue grew 12.7% in FY2024 and only marginally in FY2025 before accelerating again in 2026 [S3][S2], so industry growth is not the constraint on this name - distribution execution and input costs are.

The input side is where the sector deck does its work, and it is where we part company with the obvious reading. The agri deck prices wheat at US$294/t for FY2026 and FY2027, easing to US$284/t from FY2028, and crude palm oil at US$1,240/t against US$1,007/t in FY2025 [S0]. Those are the two lines that matter for a noodle-and-snack manufacturer: flour for the dough and sheets, frying oil for the extruded lines.

The deck's own basis resolves what looks like a gaping inconsistency between its spot field and its forward path: the forward path is built on the World Bank Pink Sheet, whose latest monthly print for wheat is US$347/t for September 2026, while the US$218/t in the spot field belongs to the futures series the deck uses for its earlier history, not to the Pink Sheet series its forward path is built on [S8][S0]. On the Pink Sheet the deck's FY2027E of US$294/t is below the latest print and above the 2025 annual average of US$243/t, and the desk's stated reading is that the September level reflects weather and competing oils rather than a level expected to persist [S0][S8]. Two consequences follow, and we take both. The base case is not carrying a conservative cost view - it is carrying a forecast that falls from the current tape. And the bull case cannot be "wheat reverts to spot", because spot is above the deck; the bull is the September premium unwinding all the way to the 2025 average, which is what we model.

Both wheat and palm are dollar-priced, so the rupiah sets the rupiah cost of a dollar input. We do not claim the model transmits that: the cost links divide a USD per tonne deck series by its own FY2025 base, so the exchange rate cancels and the forecast holds the rupiah where it is [S0]. The risks section states the size of that omission and what to do about it.

Regulation is light relative to the banks or the telcos but not irrelevant. Food products require registration and halal certification, and the plants carry food-safety certification across the manufacturing footprint [S4]. The direction of travel in Indonesian food regulation is toward front-of-pack labelling and excise on sugar-sweetened products; snacks are less exposed than beverages, but the compliance cost falls on the same plants. Nothing in the sources reviewed changes the operating economics in the forecast period [S4].

Competitive position: AISA is a challenger, not a leader. It does not disclose market share, and the categories it competes in are dominated by larger food groups with broader portfolios and deeper general-trade coverage [S4]. Its moat is narrower than a brand moat and more specific: a distributor network reaching about 193,568 outlets, factory locations that reach the main consumption island, and price points engineered to the bottom of the market [S5][S4]. That is a distribution-density moat, and the compounder test is whether it is widening - the evidence for 2026 is revenue growth by double digits in both segments while the category grew at single digits [S2]. One caveat is now stated rather than assumed: most of that revenue passes through a distributor under common control, so a widening network and a rising related-party transfer price look the same in the sales line [S3].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and structural: flour and sugar come from affiliated mills, and alternative suppliers price off the same import parity [S3]. Buyer power is high but fragmented - distributors and modern-trade buyers negotiate hard, and the affiliated distributor is by far the largest buyer [S3]. New entrants are constrained by distribution, not by capital. Substitutes are private label and cheaper regional brands, which is exactly the pressure that shows up as gross-margin volatility [S3]. Rivalry is intense and price-led at the value end [S4].

Wheat is not grown in Indonesia in commercial quantity, so the flour industry is an import-parity milling business and the price of a noodle or a biscuit is set by the world wheat price plus freight plus the rupiah. Palm oil is a domestic crop but priced off a global benchmark, and the cooking oil used by snack manufacturers trades close to that benchmark. This is why two commodity series explain most of the year-to-year variance in a food company's gross margin, and why a food analyst starts with the deck rather than with the volume line.

FY2025 is the anchor year and it was a good one: net sales of IDR1,958.0bn, a gross margin of 39.0%, operating profit of IDR131.6bn and net profit attributable to shareholders of IDR89.1bn, up on FY2024 [S3][S4]. EBITDA on the restated depreciation charge was IDR215.0bn, an 11.0% margin, and ROE was 8.1% [S3].

Two restatements of the data pack sit under that sentence and both matter. The pack carries a depreciation and amortisation charge that is a fragment of the real one: the segment note charges IDR83.4bn across cost of goods sold, selling and distribution and administration [S3]. On the pack's figure, EBITDA would be understated by more than a third and every EV/EBITDA comparison would be wrong. The pack also carries a share count of roughly two fifths of the audited figure, against the 9,312m the audited accounts and the annual report both state, which understates market capitalisation by a factor of two and a half [S3][S4]. Both are corrected in the facts file and the engine rebuilds history from them.

A third correction is not yet possible, and we state it rather than paper over it. The engine restates the share count after it has computed the market-capitalisation line, so the market capitalisation the model displays for weighting and for enterprise-value ratios is still the pack's, not ours. Everything downstream of that line is therefore wrong in the model's own output by the share-count factor: the leverage input to the cost of capital, the market-value weights, the FY2026E EV/EBITDA of 1.9x and the FCFE yield of 16.4%. Those are corrected by hand in the valuation section [S3]. The enterprise values, the DCF and the target - which is built from the DCF - rest on the audited share count and are not affected; the multiple cross-checks are affected, because the pack's own-history averages behind them are built on the same wrong count, and the basis on which we correct them is set out in the valuation section. The defect has been raised with the engine owner because it touches every restated name, not only this one [S0][S3].

The 2026 year is the one the market is reacting to. Nine-month net sales were IDR1,640.0bn, with snacks and staples both up by low-double digits, while cost of goods sold rose far faster to IDR1,070.0bn [S2]. The arithmetic is simple and painful: gross profit was flat, so the entire revenue gain was consumed by input costs, and attributable profit fell to IDR61.1bn [S2]. Our FY2026E is revenue of IDR2,187.1bn, a gross margin of 34.5%, operating profit of IDR119.2bn and net profit of IDR78.1bn, an EPS of 8.4 - the first decline after FY2025's rise from the IDR69.5bn of FY2024, and the trough of the cycle [S2][S3].

The forecast from FY2027 is a recovery in margin, not in growth. Revenue grows 7.5% in FY2027E and decelerates to 5.5% by FY2030E, roughly the nominal growth of household consumption implied by the macro deck's 3.3 rate CPI and 5.3 rate real GDP; the FY2026 step is banked and does not repeat [S2][S0]. Gross margin stays at the FY2026 trough in FY2027E because the deck holds wheat flat at its FY2026 level, then recovers to 35.5% in FY2028E and 37.1% by FY2030E as shelf prices catch up and flour eases to US$284/t [S0][S3]. Operating margin reaches 7.1% against 6.7% in FY2025 and 7.0% in FY2024; the model's peak is 7.6%, a fraction above the 2023-24 range rather than a step change, and it fades to 6.4% by FY2035E as brand and distribution spend is renewed [S3]. Net profit reaches IDR147.6bn and ROE 9.5%.

Costs. The cost links are the model's transmission mechanism: we expose a fifth of cost of goods sold to wheat and a twentieth to palm oil, and assume a pass-through of roughly a third to shelf prices, which is what the 2026 experience implies once the flour shock is run against the reported margin [S2][S3]. The pair is a calibration, not a physical measurement, and it is worth saying why: the deck's FY2025 base of US$196/t is a futures-contract average while its forward path is the Pink Sheet, whose 2025 average is US$243/t [S8]. Part of the step inside the formula is therefore a series switch, which makes the forecast's wheat headwind larger than the physical move - the cautious direction, and the reason the gross-margin input path rather than the link delivers the recovery. Selling and distribution plus administration ran at IDR629.5bn in FY2025, but that figure carries other expenses well above other income and a heavy fourth-quarter promotion; the ratio was lower in FY2024 and lower again over the first nine months of 2026, and we hold it near IDR636.4bn before drifting up as brand and distribution spend is renewed [S3][S7]. Depreciation was IDR83.4bn against capex of IDR82.5bn in FY2025; we set forecast capex a point above the depreciation charge so the asset base grows with volume instead of shrinking [S3].

Cash flow and the balance sheet. FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR22.9bn against net profit of IDR89.1bn, a poor conversion with a single explanation: IDR150.0bn was paid into an escrow account held by the anti-corruption commission in connection with criminal rulings on the legacy sukuk, booked as other non-current financial assets [S3]. Add it back and the year generated cash at roughly twice reported profit; the operating business was a strong converter and the headline number is the escrow, not the trading. Capex was IDR82.5bn, free cash flow to the firm IDR103.4bn, and net debt IDR103.7bn against EBITDA of IDR215.0bn - 0.5 times, with cash of IDR133.4bn and gross debt of IDR237.1bn [S3]. Finance cost was IDR27.5bn [S3].

Working capital is unusual and we keep it that way rather than normalising it: current liabilities exceed current assets excluding cash, because trade payables and short-term financial liabilities fund a receivable book that sits largely with the affiliated distributor [S3]. The negative working-capital ratio releases cash as revenue grows, which is a real feature of the last three years and is visible in free cash flow; a reader who prefers to assume it reverses should cut our value by roughly a tenth.

Capital allocation is conservative and we do not expect it to change quickly. Capital expenditure is maintenance-led, no acquisition or divestment has been announced, and net new borrowing is assumed at zero after the company repaid net bank debt in FY2025 [S3][S4]. The interesting question is distributions: the annual meeting resolved not to pay a dividend, and the quasi-reorganisation of July 2026 removed the accumulated deficit of IDR2,728.6bn that stood in the way [S4][S6]. We assume no dividend in FY2026E and a modest one from FY2027E. Under the cash-flow method the target rests on, the payout path does not change the value - free cash flow to the firm is struck before distributions and already charges every rupiah of capex and working capital - so a higher payout is a reason to own the stock for the cash it returns, and a signal that the group is willing to let cash leave the listed entity, rather than a reason to raise the value.

Earnings-quality flags, per the house card, starting with the one the card puts first. We could not verify AISA's IDX listing board or notation status from any source available to us: the exchange's own site is outside the fetcher's permitted scope by design, the annual report does not state the board, and no registered press item reports a notation for the name. That is an open verification item, not a clearance, and it matters more here than usual - this is the successor to Tiga Pilar Sejahtera, whose sukuk default sits behind the escrow, and the special monitoring board's full call auction would change every entry and exit assumption. Until it is confirmed we would size the position as if the special board applied [S4][S9].

Accruals are not the problem: net profit exceeded operating cash flow in FY2025 only because of the escrow payment, and in FY2024 cash flow was well above profit [S3]. The divergence flags are real, though. Trade receivables from the related party rose faster than revenue, inventory rose faster than cost of goods sold, and both are consistent with a distributor relationship in which the listed entity carries the working capital [S3]. Margin was expanding in FY2025 while cash conversion was deteriorating - the classic combination the card warns about - and conversion did not recover until the escrow payment was made. We classify this as optics-class rather than manipulation-class: it is disclosed, audited without modification by Ernst & Young Indonesia, and explained by a named related party [S3][S4]. One disclosure-timeliness item is unresolved rather than explained: the company's own financial-statements page still lists March 2026 as the latest quarterly filing, so the nine-month 2026 accounts are not on the site at the accounts date and our nine-month figures come from the press [S9][S2].

We use the compounder card's method set because the question is a durable cash-generating franchise, not a commodity producer: discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method at a sixty per cent weight, a P/E cross-check at thirty per cent and an EV/EBITDA cross-check at ten, the house weighting for food and beverage [S0]. The DCF is primary because earnings are at a trough, and a multiple on trough earnings would simply capitalise the cycle.

The cost of capital is built from the house inputs: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, an equity risk premium on the mature market with an Indonesia country premium, a bottom-up beta of 1.08 from the industry's unlevered default and the company's leverage, and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 13.0% and a WACC of 10.7%. The weights and the leverage inside that build are not what the table says they are, and the reader should know which numbers to trust: the debt-to-equity of 0.69 and the weights of 59.2% equity and 40.8% debt are computed on the data pack's market capitalisation, which the restatement defect described above leaves a factor of two and a half too small. On the corrected capitalisation the leverage is a little over a quarter, the weights are roughly four fifths equity to one fifth debt, and the WACC is about ten basis points lower than the figure displayed. The DCF is run at the displayed rate, so it is marginally conservative and the target is unaffected; what is affected is the presentation above and the two ratios named in the financial-analysis section. We have raised the defect with the engine owner rather than patching the model from inside the company folder [S0][S3].

The compounder card pins the cost of capital for an IDR name in an eleven-to-thirteen per cent band, and this build sits at its edges. The cost of equity is 13.0% - above the top of the band on the displayed capitalisation, and inside it once the beta is re-levered on the corrected weights, because most of the displayed equity cost is the leverage error rather than the risk of the business. The WACC is 10.7%, below the bottom of the band, and the reason is structural rather than a discount we have chosen: a debt weight of 40.8% at a pre-tax cost of 9.4% is cheap against an equity cost of 13.0%, and on the corrected capitalisation the debt weight falls to roughly a fifth with the WACC a shade lower still. We run the DCF at the displayed rate, so the band breach is on the conservative side of the corrected rate by about ten basis points; a lower rate would need an argument this company's leverage does not supply [S0].

The discount rate is not doing the work here; the margin and growth paths are. Our DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR1,591.8bn and a value per share of Rp169, with 53.5% of that in the terminal value - high, but this is a ten-year explicit forecast for a business whose capital intensity is close to its depreciation charge, so most of the value is by construction the steady-state cash flow rather than a growth premium.

The multiple-survival test the card demands, answered against ourselves rather than in our favour. We apply 5.7 times EBITDA in the EV/EBITDA cross-check, and the DCF's terminal value implies a little under six times FY2035E EBITDA of IDR361.5bn - roughly a twentieth more than the multiple we apply, so the DCF does carry a small amount of terminal multiple expansion and we say so rather than claim it does not. What it does not carry is growth: the terminal value capitalises a mature EBITDA at a low-single-digit perpetuity. A reader should read that expansion as the measure of how much of the target depends on a buyer paying slightly more for this business than the peer set pays today.

Growth is manufactured here, not declared, and the arithmetic is the card's. Net reinvestment is small: capex of IDR120.3bn against depreciation of IDR93.2bn, with a further cash release from working capital as revenue grows, is under a fifth of the after-tax operating profit the year earns at the 22.0% tax rate. What growth there is comes from a high incremental return on that thin capital in the recovery years, because the margin rather than the asset base does the work: net fixed assets rise from IDR1,064.5bn in FY2025A to IDR1,219.4bn by FY2030E while EBIT rises from IDR131.6bn to IDR199.4bn. That is the reinvestment-times-ROIIC test passed on the arithmetic, and it is also where the fade shows. From FY2031E the model has EBIT flat to lower (IDR220.7bn to IDR216.4bn) while the asset base keeps growing to IDR1,415.0bn, so incremental returns in the settled years fall to about the cost of capital and below it. We do not claim a widening moat that would justify more: the moat is distribution density, and the evidence that it is widening is the 2026 revenue growth that the affiliated distributor makes hard to read [S5][S3]. The terminal value is 53.5% of EV, grown at 4.0% with reinvestment assumed at the cost of capital, not at an excess return; there is no franchise premium inside it. Returns on the book fade from 8.1% in FY2025A to 9.5% by FY2030E and 7.7% by FY2035E, below the cost of equity throughout. That is the honest description of a business whose value is a margin recovery rather than a compounding machine, and it is why the sensitivity table below shows the gross margin doing more of the work than revenue growth.

The cross-checks are below the primary, and part of the gap is a measurement defect rather than a disagreement about the business. Both multiples are applied to FY2025A metrics - earnings of IDR89.1bn in the P/E leg and EBITDA of IDR215.0bn in the EV/EBITDA leg - and not to the trough year, because the engine takes the last actual as the base for both. Both target multiples are also the average of the peer median and an own-history average, and the own-history block is built by the data pack on the same share count as the market-capitalisation line - the pack's count, roughly two fifths of the audited share count of 9,312m - so both legs are understated by that factor before any judgement about the business. Corrected, and with the FY2023A observation dropped because its profit was so depressed that a restated P/E would sit in the high double digits and would lift the blend far above the DCF, the FY2024A and FY2025A own-history P/Es are each in the mid-teens; averaged with the peer median that is close to the 11.9x the model applies. That is the basis for the P/E leg, and it is a judgement stated rather than a figure copied: a reader who keeps the FY2023A year should read the P/E cross-check as above the DCF, not below it. The EV/EBITDA leg carries the share error and a second one - the pack's EBITDA is built on the fragment depreciation charge - so restated on both counts its own-history average rises by more than the share factor, to a level just below the peer median; corrected, the applied multiple is near seven times rather than the 5.7x displayed, and at that multiple the cross-check lands within a tenth of the DCF. Applied to the trough year's EPS of 8.4 the same 11.9 times would give a value about a tenth below the Rp114 displayed, so against trough earnings the gap to the DCF is wider than the table shows, not narrower: on trough earnings the P/E says the shares are worth around the current price, which is the honest statement of what a trough-capitalising buyer would pay. The conclusion is therefore narrower than a first reading: the only method that disagrees with the DCF is the one that capitalises the trough, the two own-history averages have been corrected rather than lifted, and a reader who believes the trough is permanent should value the name on the P/E leg, which is close to the current price and to the bear case.

The escrow, valued once and consistently. IDR150.0bn sits in a commission account, outside cash and outside the operating assets the DCF discounts, and it is inside the book value against which we compare the price [S3]. We carry half of the balance in the valuation bridge - the probability-weighted value of a return, on the disclosed facts that the group is not a party to the criminal case but does not control the funds - and it is therefore in every scenario that follows. Two comparisons follow, and they must use two book definitions. Against book including the escrow the shares are at 0.7x FY2026E book; against book with the escrow written to zero entirely - crediting nothing for it anywhere - the multiple is higher but still below one. Our value includes half the escrow and the market's price includes none of it: that gap is part of why the base case is above the quote, and a reader who writes the escrow to zero should cut our value by about a twentieth, not abandon the idea.

What today's price implies. At Rp97 the market capitalises FY2026E earnings at 11.6x and book value at 0.7x, and the free cash flow yield on our FY2026E FCFF of IDR77.6bn is in the high single digits on the corrected capitalisation [S0][S3]. The reverse DCF tells us which line carries the quote. It solves the revenue-growth assumption only, holding every cost, margin and terminal input at our base, and applies the same subtraction to growth in every forecast year until the DCF value per share equals the price. The answer is 1.5% for FY2027E against our 7.5%, and lower still in the years after it. So the quote is consistent with our full margin recovery and close-to-flat revenue growth for a decade; it is not consistent with the recovery failing. A variant that holds the gross-margin base at the FY2025 actual, with no shelf-price recovery at all, values the equity below the quote, so the recovery is already paid for. What is not paid for is growth, and that is where our base case earns its premium: on the same margins, restoring revenue growth to our path is most of the distance between the quote and Rp148. We underwrite that growth on distribution rather than on the 2026 sales line, because most of the sales line is billed to a related party and the nine-month split is not disclosed: the reach is documented - 193,568 outlets through the distributor groups the company appoints [S5] - while the demand behind it cannot be verified from the filings [S3]. That is the weakest link in the case and we state it as one; it is also the line the bear case attacks.

The gap between our value and the price is a governance discount we are being paid to hold, and it should be sized rather than waved away. Most of sales go to an affiliated distributor and a large slice of equity sits in an escrow account; those two facts justify a permanent discount to a clean peer, and our liquidity discount of 10.0% covers only the thin trading line, not the structure [S3][S0]. A reader who applies a further structural discount of their own should apply it to our value rather than to the market price. At a third off the base value the shares would still be worth more than they cost; the bear case, not the base, is the number to watch.

The dominant risk is not the wheat price; it is that the listed entity's economics are set by parties it does not control. Most of net sales go to PT FKS Pangan Nusantara, an entity under common control, and the receivable from that customer is among the largest assets on the balance sheet [S3]. Flour and sugar come from two more affiliates [S3]. A transfer-pricing decision at the distributor - a margin reset, a longer credit period, a change in who bears promotional cost - moves value at AISA without any change in the underlying business. Likelihood: moderate over the cycle, because the group has every incentive to keep the listed entity financeable; impact: high, because it can move earnings by more than the cyclical swing we are underwriting. It is in the bear case as a two-point rise in the operating ratio, which on its own is worth roughly a quarter of the base value; combined with the slower growth, lower margin and higher wheat of the four-shock bear it takes most of it.

Two pieces of evidence make that risk harder to dismiss than the group's incentives suggest, and one piece of evidence is missing. Sales to the affiliated distributor were IDR1,443.8bn, or 73.7% of net sales, in FY2025 against a higher share in FY2024 [S3]. So the mix does move, and it moved in the listed company's favour that year - the terms are negotiable rather than fixed, which cuts both ways. But the 2026 split is not disclosed: the nine-month accounts are not on the company's own site and the press coverage of the nine-month result gives no related-party figure, so the double-digit revenue growth cannot be decomposed into third-party demand and affiliate billing [S9][S2]. We have restated the variant view accordingly - the margin squeeze is evidenced in cost of goods sold, the demand recovery is not evidenced at all - and the risk sits in the bear case rather than only in this paragraph.

The escrow is the second discrete risk. IDR150.0bn sits in a commission escrow account pending resolution of criminal cases about the legacy sukuk [S3]. Management states the group is not a party to the case; the funds are nonetheless outside the company's control and could be confiscated or returned. We carry half of the balance in the valuation bridge, so every case in the table below includes a probability-weighted return; confiscation is therefore a further downside of that half, and the bear case is not the floor. Likelihood of loss: low-to-moderate on the disclosed facts; impact: a slice of equity of the order of a tenth of book value.

Input costs are the third, and the honest statement of it is narrower than the heading suggests. The agri deck has wheat holding at US$294/t in FY2027 against the latest Pink Sheet print of US$347/t, and with pass-through of roughly a third a further leg up in either wheat or palm oil hits margin directly [S0][S8][S3]. A weaker rupiah compounds it in the physical business, but not in this model: the cost links divide a dollar-denominated deck series by its own base, so the exchange rate cancels and the forecast assumes the rupiah stays where it is against the dollar [S0]. The omission is small at the deck's own path - the macro deck's Rp18,350/USD for FY2027 is under a percentage point above spot, and the nine-month margin we calibrate to was already earned at today's rate - but it is real if the rupiah moves: each further tenth of depreciation costs about a point of gross margin before any price response, against a recovery of only two and a half points of gross margin from the trough to FY2030E. The sensitivity table in the valuation section has no FX row because the model cannot produce one; a reader who wants the rupiah case should cut the base value by the value of that point of margin.

Then the ordinary consumer risks. Purchasing power is the volume driver for value-priced snacks, and management's own framing is that pack sizes had to be engineered down to stay affordable [S4]. A demand shock would hit a company with a thin public float of 26.1% that also fails the house investability floors: on the audited share count the market capitalisation is about nine tenths of the minimum and average daily turnover of IDR1.6bn over the last quarter is below the ADV floor, so the model's `investable` flag is false on both tests [S0]. The BUY is therefore a research view, not a sized position: the twelve-month target already carries the maximum liquidity discount of 10.0%, and taking a position at size would need a documented exception to the universe limits rather than a larger order in the market.

Base case, 50.0% probability: revenue grows 11.7% in FY2026E as the nine-month run-rate is banked, then decelerates; gross margin bottoms at the reported trough in FY2026E to FY2027E and recovers to the company's demonstrated operating level by FY2030E; value Rp148 [S2][S3]. Bear, 25.0%: the affiliated distributor resets trade terms so two points of revenue move to the distribution arm, revenue growth is three points slower, gross margin is a point and a half lower with no pass-through at all, and wheat holds the September Pink Sheet print rather than easing - value Rp47, about half the quote. Bull, 25.0%: the September premium unwinds all the way to the 2025 average, growth is three points faster and fixed-cost absorption holds the operating ratio two points lower, so gross margin gains a point and a half - value Rp332. The four shocks are mirrored pair for pair on the same wheat, growth, margin and cost drivers, at the house limit of four, and the probabilities reflect that the cost path is the reviewed house deck rather than our own extrapolation [S0][S3][S8]. The spread is wide because the base is thin: the bear takes about half the value and the bull more than doubles it, which is what a few points of gross margin does to trough operating profit. The escrow is the one element deliberately not mirrored - its return or confiscation is a one-sided event by nature, so it is carried at the same probability-weighted half in every case.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of weight: a decision on the escrow; any change in the terms of trade with the affiliated distributor disclosed in a quarterly filing; the FY2026 fourth-quarter gross margin, which tells us whether pass-through started before the year closed; and the FY2027 dividend decision. If gross margin fails to recover in the first half of 2027 while wheat is easing, the trough is structural and the P/E cross-check is the right value, which is close to today's price.

Ownership and control. PT Pangan Sejahtera Investama is the controlling shareholder with 58.4% of voting shares, inside a group structure that also holds the group's international investment vehicles; the public holds 26.1% [S4]. The board and commissioners disclosed no share ownership at the end of 2025 [S4]. Concentration of that order means minority holders cannot outvote the controller on anything, so the protections that matter are disclosure, the audit and the related-party process - not the ballot.

Related-party gravity, quantified. Sales to PT FKS Pangan Nusantara were IDR1,443.8bn in FY2025, 73.7% of consolidated net sales, down from a higher share in FY2024 [S3]. Purchases from affiliates were 6.8% of cost of goods sold for flour from Bungasari and 10.5% for sugar from Tereos FKS, with smaller lines for packaging and services [S3]. On both sides of the ledger, then, the listed company's margin is the residual of a negotiation inside one group. The receivables note shows the working-capital consequence: the affiliated customer is the largest receivable and grew faster than sales [S3]. This is the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange, and it is disclosed in full rather than buried.

The legacy. This company is the successor to Tiga Pilar Sejahtera Food, whose legacy sukuk sits at the centre of the criminal cases that produced the escrow arrangement; the annual report's change-of-name section and the audit committee's disclosure of the legal matters are the primary record [S4][S3]. The July 2026 quasi-reorganisation - capital reduction approved by shareholders in May and effective on the minister's decree in July - removed the accumulated deficit of IDR2,728.6bn and restored the company's ability to distribute [S6][S3]. We treat the clean-up as a genuine reset: executed through the proper corporate process, disclosed, and audited.

Audit and record. Ernst & Young Indonesia issued an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 accounts [S3][S4]. No dividend has been paid in the years covered by our history, and the annual meeting resolved against one [S4]. We found no disclosed pledge of the controlling stake and no rights issue or buyback since the 2020 placement; the share count has been unchanged at 9,312m [S3][S7]. Board composition and committee structure are disclosed in the annual report in the usual detail, with an audit committee and independent commissioner presence and an unqualified internal-control statement [S4]. Two items we could not close, and will not pretend to have closed: the listing board and notation status, which no source available to us discloses (see the earnings-quality paragraph), and the nine-month accounts, which are still absent from the company's own financial-statements page a fortnight past the deadline for a listed issuer third-quarter filing [S9].

ESG exposures are the ordinary ones for Indonesian packaged food. Packaging is the main waste footprint, palm oil sourcing is the main land-use exposure, and food-safety certification across the plants is the operating licence to trade [S4]. The company reports solar-panel use at its facilities and community programmes, small relative to the operating footprint [S4]. Nothing here is a valuation driver; the material governance issue is the related-party structure above, and that is where a reviewer should press.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. In practice the sequence is: the nine-month accounts, still absent from the company's own site and the first document that would show whether the related-party share moved [S9]; the FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027, which settle whether the fourth quarter continued the margin squeeze; the annual meeting in the second quarter, where the first post-reorganisation dividend decision will be taken [S4][S6]; and the first-half 2027 results, the clean read on whether price increases have started to catch up with flour while the deck's wheat path eases [S2][S0].

Between those dates we monitor four things. Gross margin quarterly, against the pass-through we assume - the single number that decides whether the DCF or the P/E cross-check is right. The related-party disclosure in each quarterly filing: the sales share to FKS Pangan Nusantara and the receivable balance, because a shift in either is the earliest warning of a transfer-pricing reset [S3]. The wheat and palm decks: the agri deck's FY2027 wheat of US$294/t now sits below the latest Pink Sheet print of US$347/t, so a deck revision toward the September tape would lower our value and a revision back toward the 2025 average of US$243/t would raise it [S0][S8]. And the escrow: any court or commission decision on the frozen funds is a discrete value event [S3].

We would revisit the rating on any of the following: a disclosed change in terms with the affiliated distributor; a dividend materially above our assumed payout, which would signal that cash is genuinely accessible to minorities; a gross-margin recovery failing to appear by the first half of 2027; or a resolution of the escrow that returns cash to the company [S3].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 11.7% is already banked: nine-month 2026 net sales were Rp1.64trn, +12.35% on 9M2025's Rp1.46trn with snacks +12.9% and staples +12.4% (F20, S2), and holding the fourth quarter at the 9M run-rate (Q4 2025 was Rp498.0bn, the FY2025 total less the nine-month figure) gives about Rp2,190bn for the year. FY2027E 7.5% then fades that step: the FY2025 base itself grew only 1.95% (S4), the growth is coming from distribution expansion - 74 distributor groups, 171 cities, about 193,568 outlets (F17, S5) - and from a low base of modern-trade penetration, which decays as coverage matures. FY2028E 6.5%, FY2029E 6.0%, FY2030E 5.5% converge on the nominal growth of household consumption: the house macro deck has 2027 CPI at 3.28% and real GDP at 5.29%, about 8.6% nominal for the economy as a whole, and a mass-market noodle and snack franchise does not outgrow that indefinitely. Long run 4.0%, below Indonesian nominal GDP, consistent with the terminal-growth ceiling in the compounder card.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 38.96% is the FY2025 audited gross margin (net sales Rp1,957.977bn, COGS Rp1,195.110bn, S3 p.18) earned with the agri deck's FY2025 average wheat of US$195.7/t and CPO of US$1,007/t. It is the base the cost links are measured from. FY2026E-27E use it unchanged, so those years show only the cost the links add - and the model then prints 34.5% and 34.3% net, against 9M2026 actual 34.8% (F20, F22, S2): the shock is the link, not a typed margin. From FY2028E the base is lifted (40.1%, 41.0%, 41.5%, 41.9% long run) to recover the part of the flour and oil step that shelf prices claw back - the company did exactly that in 2024-25, gross margin 36.8% in FY2024 rising to 39.0% in FY2025 as wheat fell (S3 p.18) - and lands net margin at about 37.5%, a point and a half below the FY2025 peak because staple foods (36% of gross sales, F13) grow faster than snacks and carry less margin. Leaving the base flat would have modelled a permanent 6-point margin loss with no price response, which no filing supports.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Crude palm oil / cooking oil at 5% of COGS. Frying oil is a real input for the extruded snack plants but is not separately disclosed and no related-party cooking-oil supplier appears in the note 6 purchase table, so the share is set at the low end of the range consistent with a snack-heavy mix (snacks were 64% of gross sales, F12).

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 0.32, the same pass-through assumed for flour: a mass-market snack at Rp2,000-10,000 a pack is sold through third-party distributors into a weak purchasing-power environment, so most of a commodity move is absorbed before it reaches the shelf price. Calibrated jointly with the flour share so the model reproduces the observed 9M2026 margin.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Wheat flour at 20% of COGS. The disclosed Bungasari flour purchases are 6.75% of COGS (F15, S3 note 6) and that is one supplier only - part of the noodle and wafer flour is bought from third-party mills and is not disclosed separately; 20% is about 3x the disclosed related-party line and is consistent with flour being the single largest material in dry noodles and wafers.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 0.32. The pair (20% share, 32% pass-through) is calibrated on the actual: the agri deck has FY2026E wheat at US$293.5/t against the deck's FY2025A base of US$195.7/t (+50%), and 20% x 0.68 x 50% = 6.8% of COGS, which with the cooking-oil link turns the 38.96% base margin into about 34.6% for FY2026E - against 9M2026 actual gross margin of 34.8% (revenue Rp1.64trn less COGS Rp1.07trn, F20, F22, S2). The pair is therefore read as the exposure the company's own reported margin implies, not as a physical wheat pass-through: the deck's FY2025A base is a Yahoo ZW=F fiscal-year average while its forward path is the World Bank Pink Sheet, whose own 2025 annual average is US$243.3/t (F35, S8), so part of the 50% step inside the formula is a series switch rather than a cost move. The consequence is conservative and is carried deliberately: the ratio is measured off a lower base than the Pink Sheet implies, so the forecast carries more wheat headwind than the physical path supports, and the gross-margin input path (not the link) is what delivers the FY2028E recovery. No price-led recovery is assumed beyond that.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025's 32.25% (gross profit Rp762.867bn less operating profit Rp131.555bn, F8, S3 p.18) is not the run-rate: it carries Rp15.4bn of other expenses against Rp8.4bn of other income and heavy fourth-quarter promotion. The operating ratio has been 29.9% in FY2024 and about 29.4% over 9M2026 (implied by the reported Rp1.64trn revenue, Rp1.07trn COGS and Rp61.09bn net profit, F20-F22, S2); Q1 2026 alone was 33.2% because first-quarter selling spend is seasonal (S7 p.8). We hold 29.1% for FY2026E and drift to 30.0% as distribution and brand investment is renewed, rather than assuming either the FY2025 peak or permanent leverage.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 4.26%, the restated FY2025 charge of Rp83.426bn on revenue of Rp1,957.977bn (F1, S3), against 4.10% in FY2024 (Rp78.681bn, F2). Held flat: the asset base is stable and capex runs close to depreciation.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 5.50%. Replacement capex is the FY2025 segment-note figure of Rp82.491bn, 4.21% of revenue (F3, S3), essentially equal to the Rp83.4bn depreciation charge. That is enough for a maintenance year but not for one in which revenue grows 74% by 2035, so we hold capex 1.3 points above D&A - about Rp45bn a year of net investment at FY2030E revenue - instead of assuming a factory that expands for free and PP&E that shrinks while volume grows. The annual report's stated capex priorities (quality, safety, cost-reduction projects, facility upgrades, S4 p.32) support the replacement base, not a step-up in new capacity.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Holdings of the history: current assets less cash less current liabilities were negative in FY2025 (Rp584.2bn less Rp133.4bn cash less Rp720.6bn current liabilities, S3 p.15-16) because trade payables and other short-term financial liabilities fund the receivable book. The negative ratio is kept rather than normalised, because the operating cycle has run this way for three years and the receivables are concentrated on a related-party customer.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 20%, between the FY2025 effective rate of 18.1% (tax Rp19.743bn on pre-tax Rp108.876bn, S3 p.18) and the 22% statutory rate, and above FY2024's 37.8% which carried a one-off prior-year adjustment.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 10.5%, the FY2025 finance cost of Rp27.487bn on opening debt of Rp262.4bn (F5, S3). Debt is bank loans plus lease liabilities plus other short-term financial liabilities (Rp78.5bn at end 2025, S3 p.16), repriced upward with the rupiah policy rate.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 2.5%, from FY2025 finance income of Rp4.808bn on opening cash of Rp222.8bn (S3).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company repaid Rp101bn of net bank debt in FY2025 (proceeds Rp100bn against Rp201bn of long-term repayments, S3 p.21) and is funding capex from operations; the quasi reorganisation was done to restore distributable reserves, not to lever up.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: other income and other expense are treated as part of the operating ratio in the forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 0.04%, the historical ratio (minority interests are a rounding item: Rp1.4bn negative balance sheet).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Nil for FY2026E: the 2025 AGMS resolved not to distribute a dividend (S4 p.87) and the quasi-reorganisation that removed the Rp2.73trn deficit only became effective on 18 July 2026 (F24, S6). A modest distribution then starts - 15% in FY2027E and 20% from FY2028E - because the stated purpose of the exercise was to restore dividend capacity for a shareholder register that is 58.4% controlled by PT Pangan Sejahtera Investama (S4 p.62), while capex and working capital still absorb most of the cash. No dividend has been declared, so this is a policy assumption, not a forecast of an announced payment.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The quasi-reorganisation reduced capital (nominal value) to eliminate the deficit; the share count stayed at 9,311,800,000 (F7, S3 p.28; AR p.62 confirms total shares 9,311,800,000), and there is no announced rights issue or buyback.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%, half the 8.6% nominal GDP the macro deck implies for Indonesia (CPI 3.28% plus real GDP 5.29%): a mature snack and noodle franchise grows with population and inflation less the ongoing share losses to private label and regional brands. The terminal margin carries the deck's long-run wheat of US$284/t, which is +45% on the deck's own FY2025A base of US$195.7/t and +17% on the World Bank Pink Sheet's 2025 average of US$243.3/t (F35, S8) - the difference is the series break described on link2_pass, and it is the cautious direction.

challenges.challenge: The report states 'we hold the position only because the price sits below even our bear-case value of Rp93' and repeats it as thesis 2. The model's bear value today is val.scenarios.bear.v0 = 92.67 against a price of 97.0: the price is 4.7% ABOVE the bear value, and the bear 12-month target of 104.74 is a +8% gain from the price. The stated reason for holding a governance-impaired name is contradicted by the model's own output; if the author meant the rolled value, the sentence carries no downside information at all.
challenges.answer: Accepted and fixed by changing the work, not the bear. The summary and thesis 2 now say the bear case is worth Rp47 against a Rp97 price (about -52%), the base Rp148 and the bull Rp332; the hold is stated as the spread between them, and the section on risks states the downside in value-per-share terms. Nothing in the report now claims the price is below the bear value. [S3]

challenges.challenge: The report names the transfer-pricing reset and the escrow confiscation as the two dominant risks, then writes 'Neither outcome is in our base case, and the bear case does not add it as a separate shock'. Thesis 5 says a transfer-pricing decision 'kills it'. The bear scenario shocks only revenue growth -3pp and gross margin -1.5pp, so the 25%-weighted downside is structurally incapable of producing the loss the report itself describes, and the probability-weighted target (167 -> 151) is built on that set.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries the named risks as shocks rather than prose. Bear has four shocks mirrored pair for pair with the bull: wheat at the September-2026 Pink Sheet print (x1.18, F34/S8) instead of easing, revenue growth -3pp, gross margin -1.5pp, and the operating ratio +2pp as the distributor margin reset. The escrow enters the valuation bridge at 50% (F19). Bear value is now Rp47 against a Rp97 price, base Rp148, bull Rp332, weighted target Rp172; the only deliberate asymmetry is the escrow, which is one-sided by nature and is disclosed as such. [S3][S8][S0]

challenges.challenge: Section 4 explains the 29%/24% divergence as 'both multiples are applied to trough earnings'. The engine passes metric = FY2025A (np_parent 89.129, EBITDA 214.981) to both methods, not FY2026E (78.05 / 212.33). On the actual trough the P/E leg is 11.86 x 78.05 / 9.3118 = Rp99, not Rp114, and the EV/EBITDA leg is Rp120. So 'a reader who believes the trough is permanent... is close to the current share price' is only true on a basis the model does not use, and the real divergence from the DCF is wider than stated.
challenges.answer: Accepted, and the correction widens the gap rather than closing it. Section 4 now states that the engine applies FY2025A metrics to both legs (NP 89.129, EBITDA 214.981), gives the trough-year equivalent (the same multiple on FY2026E EPS is about a tenth below the Rp114 displayed, i.e. around the current price), and rewrites the conclusion so the divergence is explained by the earnings basis of the P/E leg plus a share-count defect in the EV/EBITDA leg, not by a claim that both use trough earnings. [S0][S3]

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says 'the engine rebuilds history from them', but the restatement does not flow through. market.mcap_rep = 369.15 (= 3,805.72m x 97), while shares_m = 9,311.8 and the true cap is 903.2. That gives val.coc.de = 0.6895 (debt/369.15) and weights we/wd = 59.2/40.8, presented as 'at market weights' when the market weight is 78.0/22.0; the displayed FY2026E EV/EBITDA of 1.94x and FCFE yield of 16.4% are wrong by 2.45x; and own-history P/E 13.55 and EV/EBITDA 3.89 - the numbers the 11.86x and 5.75x are averaged with - come from the pack's 3,805.7m count (FY2025A own P/B 0.445 implies BVPS 300.9). Recomputed correctly, WACC is 10.62% vs 10.72%, so the DCF is not inflated, but the cross-checks and the cost-of-capital presentation are.
challenges.answer: Accepted in substance; the market-capitalisation line itself cannot be patched from the company folder because it is computed in cov_engine.market() before the restated share count is applied, so it is raised to the Director as an engine defect affecting every restated name. Sections 3 and 4 now disclose it and give the corrected figures: leverage about a quarter rather than 0.69, weights roughly four fifths equity to one fifth debt rather than 59/41, WACC about ten basis points lower than the 10.7% displayed, and an own-history EV/EBITDA average understated by about two and a half turns. The own-history P/E is price-based and unaffected; the DCF runs at the displayed rate, so it is marginally conservative. [S3][S0]

challenges.challenge: The report leans on 'the agri deck carries wheat at US$294/t against a spot of US$218/t, so the model's cost pressure is the house view rather than a bear assumption', and the whole bull narrative is 'wheat normalises toward the US$218/t spot'. The deck's own basis text says 'Spot 347.0 is the September-2026 Pink Sheet monthly print' - a 59% gap from the 217.98 Yahoo field the report quotes. If the tape is 347, the deck's FY2027E 293.5 is 15% BELOW spot, not 26% above it, and the base case's FY2027 margin is optimistic, not conservative; the bull case's premise disappears.
challenges.answer: The spot conflict is resolved against the number the report was using. Registered the World Bank Pink Sheet October-2026 release as an industry source [S8] and added the September-2026 wheat print of US$347.0/t (F34) and the 2025 annual average of US$243.3/t (F35). The agri deck's FY2027E of US$293.5 sits below the latest print and above the 2025 average, so the base case is not carrying a conservative cost view, and the bull can no longer be a reversion to spot. The bull is re-cut to the September premium unwinding to the 2025 average, sections 2 and 5 say so, and the monitoring claim that a deck revision toward spot would raise our value is reversed. Flagged to the Director: the deck's FY2025A base of US$195.7 is a futures average, not the Pink Sheet, contrary to its own basis text. [S8][S0]

challenges.challenge: Section 2 says 'both are dollar-denominated, so the rupiah matters twice', and section 5 lists rupiah weakness as a risk with the deck at 18,350 for FY2027. The cogs formula is revenue*(1-gm)*(1+share*(1-pass)*(div(d.agri.cpo,base)-1)+...), and the deck series are USD/t, so the ratio cancels FX: the model transmits zero rupiah depreciation. From FY2025A 16,448 to FY2027E 18,350 is +11.6%; at a 25% combined commodity share and 32% pass-through that is roughly 2pp of gross margin never charged to the base case, against a recovery of only +2.6pp from the trough to FY2030E.
challenges.answer: Confirmed in the template: cogs uses a ratio of the deck series to its own base, so USD/IDR cancels and the forecast transmits no rupiah move. The claim that the rupiah matters twice is deleted and sections 2 and 5 now state that the forecast holds the rupiah at spot. The magnitude is smaller than the challenge implies, and section 5 says why: the calibration anchor is the nine-month 2026 margin earned at today's rate and the macro deck's FY2027 rate of 18,350 is under a percentage point above spot, so the uncharged depreciation is a fraction of a gross-margin point, not two. The exposure is disclosed as each further tenth of depreciation costing about a point of gross margin; the sensitivity table has no FX row because the model cannot produce one. [S0][S2][S3]

challenges.challenge: The Rp150.0bn escrow (S3 p.76, verified exactly) is treated three inconsistent ways: it is inside the book value used for the 'below restated book' argument (13% of book, Rp16.1/share), it is in neither the base value nor valuation.bridge (bridge_items is empty, so equity = EV - 98.663 net debt), and section 5 says it could be confiscated without the bear case deducting it. On a book excluding the escrow the P/B is 0.91x, not 0.79x.
challenges.answer: The escrow is now in valuation.bridge at a stated probability of 50%, value Rp150.0bn, source S3 and fact F19, so it is inside the base value and every scenario rather than only inside book. Section 4 sets the two book definitions side by side: a fraction of FY2026E book including the escrow, and still below one times book with the escrow written to zero, and states that writing it to zero cuts our value by about a twentieth; section 5 states that confiscation is a further downside of the probability-weighted half, so the bear is not the floor. [S3]

The lift lands net margin at 37.1% in FY2030E and 36.4% in FY2035E - still below the 39.0% of FY2025A. Precedent for the recovery is in the LK: gross margin went from 36.8% in FY2024A to 39.0% in FY2025A on a 7% fall in the deck's wheat price (S3 p.18). Holding the base flat would model a permanent six-point margin loss with no price response, which is the unsourced haircut the base-case card forbids.

flags.message: expected return +77%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The +77% expected return is not a re-rating call and it is not a claim that the downside is small: (i) FY2026 earnings are at a cost-cycle trough - nine-month net profit fell 13.77% on COGS up 19.94% (F21, F22, S2) - so the DCF discounts a recovery to the 7.0-7.3% EBIT margins the LK shows for FY2023-24, peaking a fraction above that range in FY2031E before fading, not a step change to a new margin level (S3); (ii) what the reverse DCF says the price implies is narrower than a no-recovery call: the engine solves the revenue-growth line only, holding the full base margin path, and lands at 1.5% for FY2027E against the 7.5% base, with the same 6.0pp subtraction applied to every forecast year. The margin recovery is therefore already in the quote - a variant that holds the gross-margin base at the FY2025 actual with no shelf-price recovery, terminal included, values the equity near Rp84, below the Rp97 price. What the market does not pay for is growth, and that is where the base case's premium sits: the quote needs revenue growth close to flat for a decade, against a base case built on documented distribution expansion - 74 distributor groups, 171 cities and about 193,568 outlets (F17, S5). That growth is the weakest evidence in the case because most sales pass through the affiliated distributor (F14, F26, S3), which is why the bear case carries the distributor reset; (iii) the bear case is worth Rp47, about half the price of Rp97, and the bull case Rp332 - the target is the probability-weighted middle of a genuinely wide distribution, because at a trough operating margin a few points of gross margin doubles or halves EBIT. The bear carries the two dominant risks - a two-point operating-ratio reset at the affiliated distributor (F14, F26, S3 note 6) and wheat holding the September-2026 Pink Sheet print (F34, S8) - and the escrow enters every case at half its balance through the valuation bridge (F19). The 9M2026 cost data and the 2024-25 margin precedent (S3 p.18) support the recovery the price already pays for; the distribution data are what support the growth it does not.
